summary: Illidan Stormrage's seat, in Shadowmoon Valley. It was the Temple of Karabor first — the draenei's holiest site, designed by Exarch Hataaru and built on the strongest ley line nexus on Draenor — and it has been taken, renamed and defiled by four powers since.
history: Velen sheltered at Karabor, and when the orcs came for the draenei the temple held out against Gul'dan's assault. So the Shadow Council did something worse: they called on the Dark Star, and a column of Void energy came down on Karabor, killing many defenders instantly and driving others mad. Velen got the survivors to the harbour. The building was black afterwards and the name stuck. The Shadow Council ruled from it; Mannoroth was first summoned to Draenor here, and it was in the courtyard pool that the pit lord's blood was shed for the curse the orcs later drank at the Throne of Kil'jaeden. Ner'zhul used it as a fortress and tore the world apart from it. Magtheridon seized it when Outland was all that remained, and Illidan took it off Magtheridon with the Twin Blades of Azzinoth. Kil'jaeden then appeared to punish Illidan for failing to destroy the Lich King, and he came back from Icecrown beaten by Arthas and stayed. Akama, who had served him, opened the way in for Maiev Shadowsong and everyone behind her.
assumes: It assumes you know Illidan lost. He is not building toward anything here — he came back from Icecrown defeated, replaying it in his head, and has been sitting in a stolen fortress waiting for whoever comes next.
disputed: The wiki flags its own page as an unfinished merge of two articles that needs checking, and its RPG section credits Ner'zhul with raising the building, which does not fit the draenei history above it.
Whether Karabor was named after K'ara, the fallen naaru the orcs called the Dark Star, is marked as speculation rather than settled.

summary: Blackwing Lair is cut into Upper Blackrock Spire, in the top half of the same mountain Ragnaros held from below. It is Nefarian's laboratory, where Deathwing's son bred dragons by crossing the blood of every flight.
history: Blackrock Mountain held two powers who tolerated each other and nothing more: Ragnaros in the fire below, and above him Nefarian with what was left of the black dragonflight. Nefarian stayed out of sight for over a decade, leaving the Dark Horde under Rend Blackhand to hold the Spire in exchange for promises of dragon support he never meant to keep. What he actually wanted was his father's abandoned project. He took captive dragons of the other flights and worked their blood together, and after years of clutches dying in the shell a few of the chromatic brood began to survive. Moira Thaurissan, watching from the ruined Dark Iron court below and expecting Nefarian to come for her people next, made sure Orgrimmar heard that the Dark Horde had sworn itself to Deathwing's son. Horde champions killed Rend at the Spire, then cut through the laboratories and the twisted things in them and killed Nefarian, and carried his head back to Orgrimmar. After the Cataclysm the Twilight's Hammer recovered his corpse and raised it, and he rebuilt further down in Blackwing Descent.
assumes: It assumes you know who Nefarian is and why a dragon keeps a laboratory. He is Deathwing's son, finishing an experiment his father began and failed at, in a mountain that already belonged to a fire elemental.
disputed: The wiki hedges the experiments in its own voice: Nefarian's intentions are known, his methods remain a mystery, and it is only believed that he was blending the blood of the dragonflights.

summary: A cave north of Ruuan Weald in the Blade's Edge Mountains, held by Gruul the Dragonkiller, overlord of the gronn, and by the ogres who worship him as a god. Two encounters, twenty-five people, and no attunement of any kind.
history: Deathwing found the Dark Portal and Draenor long before anyone on Azeroth was looking, and judged the place safe enough that he scattered clutches of black dragon eggs across it under light guard. He was wrong about Blade's Edge. The gronn who live in that range pulled the guardian dragons out of the sky, and Gruul impaled the wyrms he beat himself on the stone spires the mountains are named for — which is where the epithet came from and why the skyline is what it is. The ogres of Blade's Edge took him for a deity and have worshipped him ever since. His sons range across the spires and down onto the plains of Nagrand, and High King Maulgar holds the approach to the lair with his own council of ogre lords. Nobody in Outland had provoked him and he had not moved against either faction. The reasoning for going in first was simply that his strength and his experience would be an unanswerable problem for the Horde or the Alliance if he ever decided to use them.
assumes: The bones on the spires are the whole story and the raid never tells it. They are Deathwing's, left in Blade's Edge with too few guards, and killing them is what made a gronn into a god.

summary: The Scourge's greatest fortress, raised in saronite around the Frozen Throne on the Icecrown Glacier — a cathedral of blades and claws the size of a city, wrapped in layer after layer of cursed metal. It is the last raid of Wrath of the Lich King and the end of Arthas Menethil.
history: Kil'jaeden threw Ner'zhul's prison at Azeroth and it struck this glacier. As the Lich King's reach spread, the Scourge and the nathrezim built the citadel around the throne. Arthas Menethil and Illidan Stormrage then fought each other for it in the wake of the Third War; Arthas won, shattered the ice and merged with Ner'zhul, and death knights were trained in these halls for years afterwards. Tirion Fordring's strike force came in from above: Horde and Alliance gunships dropped their forces at separate points, and the invaders cut in as far as the Halls of Reflection before the Lich King met them himself and drove them out. The Argent Crusade broke the gates for the second attempt, at heavy cost. At the throne the Lich King tore souls out of his attackers with Frostmourne, froze Tirion where he stood and began raising the dead. Tirion broke loose and shattered Frostmourne with the Ashbringer; every soul in the blade came out at once, Terenas Menethil raised the fallen, and Arthas died. Bolvar Fordragon, hanging in chains above the throne, took the helm so the Scourge would not be left masterless.
assumes: Nearly everything. Who Arthas was, what Frostmourne did to him, why a paladin is hanging in chains over the throne — the raid assumes Warcraft III, the death knight starting experience and the whole Wrath campaign, and explains none of it to anyone arriving cold.
disputed: The wiki calls Angrathar the Wrathgate the citadel's southern entrance, while the Dragonblight page treats the same gate as that zone's barred way into Icecrown. Both descriptions are on the wiki; they are looking at it from opposite sides.

The exterior was redesigned in patch 3.3.0 when the raid opened — a taller, more cylindrical spire with a platform of ice added at the top — so the citadel players flew past for the expansion's first year is not the building the entrance now sits in.

summary: Karazhan is Medivh's tower in southern Deadwind Pass, standing on a nexus of ley lines and sealed since the day its master died. It reopened full of ghosts, afterimages and demons, with the Guardian's magic still running through the walls.
history: Aegwynn built the tower in secret roughly six hundred years before the First War, on ground an older catastrophe had already weakened, wanting both a refuge from a Council she had stopped trusting and a tap into the ley lines beneath. Her son Medivh inherited it. Possessed by Sargeras, he threw parties for the nobility while the Dark Portal was opened behind the pretence, and when Aegwynn came to confront him the duel shook the tower to its foundations. Losing, he drained the life out of nearly everyone inside to feed his own strength, then banished his mother rather than kill her, leaving the place stocked with its own dead. Khadgar and Anduin Lothar killed him not long after and the tower sealed itself, and the curse spread out over Deadwind Pass and the region now called Duskwood. Kirin Tor mages picked the ruin over and took Atiesh away; the Violet Eye were set to watch what was left. When it opened again their own agents were trapped inside and dying, demons had already got in through what is effectively a beacon into the Twisting Nether, and Prince Malchezaar held the top.
assumes: Karazhan assumes you know who Medivh was — the last Guardian of Tirisfal, possessed by Sargeras, the man who opened the Dark Portal and started the First War — and that the ghosts are his household. The raid furnishes the place as though you had already grieved for it and never once says so.
disputed: The wiki flags parts of the tower's origin as speculation, including Medivh's own theory that the crater and the tower only ever existed because he would one day live there.
It also says every ley line on Azeroth converges under Karazhan, then notes in the next breath that this stopped being true once Malygos redirected them to the Nexus.
The tower's inhabitants are probably not killed permanently. Moroes, the Curator and Terestian Illhoof have all been fought again since, which the wiki records as a likelihood rather than a fact.

summary: The lowest wing on the western side of Hellfire Citadel, entered opposite the other three. A pit lord who once ruled almost all of Outland is chained inside it, kept just short of death so that his blood can be drained.
history: After the Legion came to Outland, Magtheridon held everything but a few pockets of it, and it caught him badly off guard when Illidan Stormrage and his allies took the Black Temple off him. Most people assumed the pit lord had died in that fighting. He had not. Illidan had discovered that Magtheridon's blood does something specific to orcs — it corrupts and transforms them — and so the beaten annihilan was dragged to Hellfire Citadel rather than finished. He has been there since, held by chains both physical and magical, while Illidan's minions bleed him daily and pool what they take. What it is for is standing outside on the Hellfire Peninsula: the fel orcs are manufactured here. Anyone who has run the Blood Furnace has already seen him without being told, because he is chained in the chamber directly beneath the room where Keli'dan the Breaker is fought, which is the same operation one floor up. The raid itself is short — a handful of guards and then the prisoner.
assumes: It assumes you know that Illidan Stormrage rules Outland and that the fel orcs overrunning Hellfire Peninsula are made rather than born. The prisoner in the chains is the factory, and the raid never connects the two out loud.

summary: The Molten Core is the bottom of Blackrock Depths, where the rock gives out and a lake of fire begins. It is a rift onto the Firelands and the seat of Ragnaros the Firelord, and the Dark Iron dwarves working the mountain above it are his property rather than his allies.
history: About two centuries before the Dark Portal, near the end of the War of the Three Hammers, the Dark Iron leader Sorcerer-Thane Thaurissan reached for elemental power to finish his enemies. Grief for his dead wife drove the spell past what he intended: it breached the Firelands and pulled Ragnaros bodily into the world. The eruption shattered the Redridge Mountains and raised Blackrock Mountain over the wound, and the Firelord withdrew into the burning heart of it and put the surviving Dark Irons to work. Generations later, Emperor Dagran Thaurissan's death left his widow Moira ruling a court in chaos, and rather than fight the elementals she spread word across Azeroth that Blackrock Mountain held riches and an army in the making. The Hydraxian Waterlords, elementals of water and natural enemies of fire, took up the invitation and paid champions to go down. Those raiders worked through the Core, doused the runes of warding that shielded the lake, broke Majordomo Executus, and forced Ragnaros back to the Elemental Plane. The Dark Irons were free. The rift is still there.
assumes: The raid never says why dwarves live in a volcano. Ragnaros was summoned by their own leader during a dwarven civil war two hundred years earlier, and they have belonged to him ever since; the Hydraxian Waterlords who pay you are elementals recruiting mortals for a feud of their own.
disputed: Which Thaurissan summoned Ragnaros is told two ways on the same page. The history credits the Sorcerer-Thane at the end of the War of the Three Hammers; the quoted game guide credits Emperor Thaurissan, who is a much later descendant.
Ragnaros was banished rather than destroyed, which is how he is available to be fought again in the Firelands. The wiki uses defeat and banishment interchangeably for what happens here.

summary: Kel'Thuzad's flying necropolis, hanging over the Carrion Fields in the Dragonblight. Four quarters and a frostwyrm lair, functioning at once as a torture house, a workshop and a military academy for death knights.
history: Kel'Thuzad went north to answer the Lich King's call and was let inside Naxxramas, where Anub'arak walked him through four wings stacked with plague cauldrons and supplies. What he understood from it — that the Lich King was preparing a war on everything living — frightened him enough to try to teleport out, and he was intercepted before he got anywhere. Ner'zhul took his oath and handed him the necropolis, along with a vision of cultists tearing it out of the ground and putting it in the sky. It first appeared over the Plaguelands, warded so heavily nobody could enter until the Argent Dawn adapted an old Kirin Tor cloaking cantrip. Darion Mograine went in to free his father's trapped soul and met the Four Horsemen, whose leader turned out to be Alexandros Mograine himself; almost everyone with him died. Bolvar Fordragon later sent Alliance heroes who cut through to Kel'Thuzad and killed him, and the necropolis drifted back to Northrend. It has returned over the Dragonblight with him seated in it again. The Scourge credit an architect named Obrahiim as pivotal to its design.
assumes: The Naxxramas you can enter is the second one. The first stood over the Plaguelands, took forty people at level sixty, and moved; the Adventure Guide's version is the Northrend rebuild, and nothing inside it explains what happened the first time or who Kel'Thuzad was to begin with.
disputed: The wiki keeps the Classic necropolis on a separate page and treats this as a distinct instance rather than a retuning, which is a decision about what counts as the same raid rather than a fact about the place.
The Classic-era account is flagged as an incomplete stub pending the Ashbringer comic, so how much of Darion Mograine's raid is canon in its current form is not settled on the page itself.

summary: A cave under the Dragonmurk in Dustwallow Marsh, its entrance carved to look like the broodmother's own open mouth. Onyxia went to ground here after she was unmasked in Stormwind, and it is the smallest raid in the game.
history: Onyxia is Deathwing's daughter and Nefarian's sister, and where her father used force and her brother used laboratories, she used politics. Living in Stormwind as the noblewoman Katrana Prestor, she worked to hollow the kingdom out from inside: she set the Defias Brotherhood against it, and when King Varian Wrynn sailed for Theramore she worked a ritual meant to strip his will away from him and leave a pliable king behind. That half of him escaped into the sea and washed up in Kalimdor with no memory of who he was. With Varian missing his son Anduin was crowned, Bolvar Fordragon was made regent lord, and Onyxia kept her seat at court through all of it. Marshal Windsor eventually exposed her, and she fled to the lair she had built in the marsh: a magma-lined cut in the ground below the Dragonmurk, ceiling groaning and shifting overhead, walls spilling lava where the heat could not be held, guarded by black dragonspawn and her own whelps. She was killed there. Her brood was still living in the cave years later.
assumes: It assumes you have already met her. The whole point of Onyxia is the years she spent running Stormwind's court as a human noblewoman, and none of that is anywhere in the cave.
disputed: There are two Onyxia's Lairs on the wiki. The original was a forty-player level-sixty raid released with the game; this page is the ten and twenty-five player version retuned at level eighty for the fifth anniversary in patch 3.2.2.
The dragon on the loading screen is not Onyxia. It is an image of Alexstrasza taken from the RPG book Shadows and Light.

summary: The Ruins are the outer city of Ahn'Qiraj, the part of the qiraji capital left standing open to the sky in southern Silithus after the War of the Shifting Sands. When the gates were reopened it was where the Horde held the line while the Alliance went underneath.
history: A thousand years ago the night elves and the dragonflights drove the qiraji back to their own capital and met a concentration of silithid at its gates that they could not break. Rather than win, they sealed: the barrier went up, and the city was left in ruins behind it. The qiraji spent the next thousand years breeding. When the Twilight's Hammer, led by the ogre mage Cho'gall, worked a ritual from outside the Scarab Wall that reached the chamber where C'Thun lay chained, the Old God woke and threw its armies at Silithus. Anachronos recognised what had stirred and knew the empire would only get stronger. With the Scepter of the Shifting Sands reassembled out of fragments scattered across the world, the gates opened and the qiraji poured out. Varok Saurfang, given command of a joint campaign by Thrall and the regent lord of Stormwind, split the assault: his own elite would take the ruined outer city and hold the swarms there while the Alliance descended into the temple below. This is that outer city, and Ossirian the Unscarred is what was holding it.
assumes: It assumes you know why a wall was ever needed. The night elves fought this war a thousand years ago and did not win it, and the reputation the entire loot system runs on belongs to the Cenarion Circle because they are the ones who have been watching the hives ever since.
disputed: Who raised the barrier is told two ways on the same page. One account credits the night elves and all four dragonflights; the other credits the night elves and the bronze dragonflight with help from some of the Aspects' children.
The RPG material goes further and says nobody remembers whether the Scarab Wall was built by the elves to keep the qiraji in or by the qiraji to keep the elves out.

summary: The raid wing of Coilfang Reservoir, under Zangarmarsh, where Lady Vashj runs the operation that is draining the marsh above. It is a cavern of bridges and platforms over open water, and she prefers it to anywhere else Illidan could have put her.
history: When Illidan Stormrage called for help after the Third War, a body of naga under Lady Vashj answered, and she has been his most dedicated lieutenant since. Whoever controls the water controls Outland: his words to her, and the reason Coilfang Reservoir exists. The pumps here are taking Zangarmarsh apart above ground, and Vashj oversees the draining personally rather than sit in the cold stone of the Black Temple. Her court is not only naga. Hydross the Unstable is a bound water elemental at the entrance, Leotheras the Blind is a demon hunter who lost the argument with what was inside him, Morogrim Tidewalker is a sea giant, and Fathom-Lord Karathress commands her captains. The Lurker Below has to be fished out of its own pool rather than pulled. Held in Karathress's chamber was Seer Olum, a Broken prisoner, and it was Olum who got word to Akama that Kael'thas Sunstrider had already stopped being loyal — which is how the Black Temple's own door came to be opened later.
assumes: It assumes somebody already told you what Coilfang is for. The machinery here is why the marsh overhead is dying, and the raid never mentions Zangarmarsh at all.
disputed: Whether Vashj serves Illidan or only herself is a question the wiki raises about her and then deliberately leaves open.

summary: The plateau the Highborne raised around the Sunwell when they made it, on the Isle of Quel'Danas north of Silvermoon. The Legion came back to use the drained fount as a doorway, and this is the raid that closed it.
history: Around six thousand eight hundred years before the Dark Portal, Dath'Remar Sunstrider poured a stolen vial of the Well of Eternity into a lake sitting on a ley line convergence, and his followers built the plateau around what came up out of it. The Scourge took it during the Third War: Dar'Khan Drathir dropped the shields for Arthas, killed members of the Convocation of Silvermoon inside the plateau, and bound the well's energies for his new masters. Kael'thas Sunstrider destroyed it himself rather than let it corrupt what was left of his people. Years later the Legion returned to the island to open a gateway through the ruined fount, and the Shattered Sun Offensive formed at Shattrath to stop them. Champions fought up through Legion demons, Sunfury and felblood elves, freed the blue dragon Kalecgos from the dreadlord Sathrovarr, and killed the imprisoned naaru M'uru. Kil'jaeden rose out of the well itself; Anveena Teague spent the last of herself against him, and the weakened demon was banished and the gate shut. Velen then found a spark left in M'uru's heart and relit the Sunwell with it, as Light as well as arcane.
assumes: It assumes the whole blood elf story. The well at the centre is why their race is named what it is and why they were starving for magic, Kael'thas destroyed it with his own hands before this, and the raid never mentions that the demon at the end is the one who made the Lich King.
disputed: The wiki's account is written from the Alliance side — Alliance adventurers infiltrating the plateau — for a raid both factions ran under the same banner.
Kil'jaeden was banished, not killed, and the wiki credits the turn to Anveena Teague's sacrifice rather than to the raid, which leaves who actually beat him unresolved.

summary: The Temple is the inner city: a complex built before anyone was writing anything down, part monument to gods nobody names and part breeding ground for the qiraji army. Underneath it is the vault where C'Thun was chained, which makes this the only place in Classic where an Old God can be reached at all.
history: The War of the Shifting Sands ended not with the qiraji beaten but with them shut in. The barrier held the Twin Emperors Vek'lor and Vek'nilash inside their own temple for a thousand years, and the dragons who paid for that seal were left weakened or, later, enslaved within it. C'Thun, chained below, was freed when the Twilight's Hammer worked a ritual from outside the Scarab Wall that pierced into the prison chamber; the energy released killed most of the cultists who cast it and left the survivors catatonic in the desert. Once the Scepter of the Shifting Sands opened the gates, the Horde was given the ruins above and the Alliance the descent. They fought down through the hives and through C'Thun's own servants — the Prophet Skeram, the emperors, the things kept in the pits — and into the vault. Their march was described afterwards as a path of madness; men came out with their bodies mostly intact and their minds much less so. An Old God was killed, and both the Aspects and the Old Gods still buried elsewhere took the point.
assumes: It assumes the gates were opened, once, by somebody. On every realm a single player assembled the Scepter of the Shifting Sands and rang the gong, in a server-wide war effort that has not run since and cannot be repeated; the raid begins after that has already happened.
disputed: The wiki's account of the Ahn'Qiraj War is flagged as an unfinished stub pending Chronicle Volume 3. What it does say — Alliance into the temple, Horde into the ruins — is a summary of Blizzard's own retelling rather than a division of labour anybody was held to in play.
Whether the qiraji were ever defeated or merely contained is left deliberately unresolved by the sources: the same event is described as imprisonment behind a barrier and as the end of the war.

summary: Less a place than a night. This is the last battle of the Third War replayed out of the Caverns of Time: night elves, Alliance and Horde holding three bases on the slopes while Archimonde climbs toward the World Tree, and the raid is fought inside a time pocket disconnected from history.
history: By the time the Legion's second invasion reached Kalimdor it had already broken every nation in the Eastern Kingdoms and killed Cenarius. Archimonde wanted the second Well of Eternity beneath Nordrassil; with its power he could open a gateway wide enough to bring Sargeras through. Medivh, at the end of his own story, brought three factions who did not want to be allies into one line. Jaina Proudmoore's base fell first, then Thrall's, both commanders meeting Archimonde in person and being teleported clear at the last moment; Broxigar held a pass and was the only one of his company to walk out of it. The night elves gave ground last, thousands of them dying to buy the summit time. At the top Malfurion Stormrage called the wisps to Nordrassil and set off the tree's enchantments, and the blast destroyed Archimonde and nearly every demon and undead on the continent. It cost the night elves their immortality, which they had agreed in advance to spend. The Lich King used the defeat to cut himself loose from the Legion, and Medivh, satisfied the world no longer needed a Guardian, left it.
assumes: The raid assumes Warcraft III. It drops you into the middle of a battle whose participants, stakes and ending are all established in a game you cannot play from here, and because it happens in a sealed time pocket, nothing you do in it changes anything.
disputed: The date moved. Blizzard's first published timeline put the battle in year 20; the World of Warcraft cinematic and a Burning Crusade quest both place it in 21, and 21 is what the wiki now uses.

What actually killed Archimonde has been told several ways. Earlier accounts had druids feeding the tree their people's immortality along with the gathered energy of uncounted spirits; the Ultimate Visual Guides say wisps surrounded him. Chronicle Volume 3 settles the Legion's objective as the second Well of Eternity rather than the tree itself.
The instance was originally hinted to be an Infinite dragonflight attack on the timeline. That was dropped in favour of a time pocket disconnected from history.
Kaz'rogal, one of the four demon commanders fought here, does not appear in Warcraft III at all.

summary: Malygos's own chamber at the top of the Nexus on Coldarra, and a raid with exactly one thing in it. The Aspect of Magic decided that mortals could not be trusted with the arcane and set about taking it back from them.
history: Malygos came out of ten thousand years of madness with a purpose: the Kirin Tor and every other mortal spellcaster had been abusing magic since the Well of Eternity, and it was going to stop. He redirected Azeroth's ley lines into the Nexus and began draining the world's arcane, killing mages who objected — and taking in some of the Kirin Tor who did not, which was the part Dalaran had not expected. The city picked itself up and moved into the sky over Northrend to fight him, and still could not manage it alone. At Wyrmrest Temple the other flights met, heard what he had become, and reluctantly concluded he was past saving; Alexstrasza, who thought of him as a brother, agreed to it anyway, and the agreement became the Wyrmrest Accord. The red flight carried mortals into the Eye of Eternity itself, where the fight ends on hovering discs above an open platform, and Malygos was killed there. The Kirin Tor spent years afterwards putting the ley lines back. What nobody had an answer for is that killing him left the world's magic with no Aspect appointed to watch it.
assumes: It assumes you already accept that killing him is the right answer. Malygos is not corrupted, not possessed and not wrong about what mortals did with magic — he is an Aspect doing his job past the point of reason, and the raid is the other dragons voting to put him down.
disputed: Thrall: Twilight of the Aspects tells Arygos's death here differently from the game. In the novel he is killed in the Eye by an alternate-timeline Aedelas Blackmoore, and his blood is what activates the Focusing Iris. The wiki records both versions side by side rather than choosing.

Until patch 4.2.0 the fight could not be started at all without the Key to the Focusing Iris, a Sapphiron drop out of Naxxramas, so the raid was gated behind a different raid rather than behind anything in its own story.

summary: The Eye is the inner sanctum of Tempest Keep, hanging in the Netherstorm. The naaru built the fortress and can move it between dimensions; Kael'thas Sunstrider took it and set his court up at its heart.
history: Tempest Keep was made by the naaru, beings of pure energy and the Legion's oldest enemies, and it is more than a base — the structure can teleport itself between dimensions in a blink. Kael'thas Sunstrider took it from them. Having destroyed his own people's corrupted Sunwell rather than leave it in Scourge hands, and then brought the survivors to Outland and bound them to Illidan, he installed himself in the Eye at the fortress's core and left the three outlying wings — the Arcatraz, the Botanica and the Mechanar — to subordinates. Sunfury blood elves fill it: astromancers under High Astromancer Solarian in the Solarium, bloodwarders on the bridges, and in the Phoenix Hall the phoenix Al'ar, which is his. In the Crucible stands the Void Reaver, a Legion construct. Killing Al'ar was part of what Akama used to persuade Illidan that he was still loyal. At the end of it Kael'thas waits on the Tempest Bridge with four advisors — Thaladred the Darkener, Lord Sanguinar, Grand Astromancer Capernian and Master Engineer Telonicus — and a fortress that can leave.
assumes: The raid never explains what Kael'thas is. He is the last Sunstrider, the prince who destroyed his people's own Sunwell to save them from it, and by the time you reach him he is working for the Legion behind Illidan's back — a betrayal revealed in Serpentshrine Cavern, not here.
disputed: The raid apparently went by the name Eye of the Storm while it was in development, and that name was printed on the Outland map published in the Burning Crusade Townhall.
In game and out, this raid is usually just called Tempest Keep, though the name properly covers the whole complex, including the three five-player dungeons.

summary: The black dragonflight's room in the Chamber of Aspects beneath Wyrmrest Temple, reached down a crack in the ice off the Path of the Titans. Sartharion is standing over a clutch of twilight eggs, with three drakes in side chambers who will join him if you leave them alive.
history: Neltharion went into hiding after the other Aspects drove him out, but the flight he left behind kept working. Hunted and dwindling, it first tried simply to breed its numbers back; then its agents began crossing the blood of other dragonflights, and what came out of that was the twilight dragons. Those were believed destroyed after an attack on Grim Batol. In the wake of the Nexus War, with Alexstrasza setting her children to look for treachery inside the Wyrmrest Accord's own house, they found a fresh clutch of twilight eggs sitting in the black flight's chamber directly under the temple. The Accord was already stretched between the Scourge and the blue dragonflight, so Korialstrasz sent word to Dalaran's Council of Six and asked for mortal adventurers instead of dragons. They went down and destroyed the brood. Sartharion the Onyx Guardian stood over it with Shadron, Tenebron and Vesperon in the side chambers, and a raid could clear the drakes first or leave any of them alive, which made the fight and the reward heavier together. The black flight retaliated by attacking the Ruby Sanctum next door.
assumes: It assumes you know what a twilight dragon is and why a clutch of them under the dragons' own capital is alarming. The Chamber of Aspects has a room for each flight, and this is the room nobody was watching.

summary: The red dragonflight's chamber in the Chamber of Aspects under Wyrmrest Temple, a door along from the Obsidian Sanctum. One boss, and the first sight of what the Cataclysm was going to be.
history: When adventurers destroyed the twilight eggs in the Obsidian Sanctum it was done fast and quietly, without fanfare and without much acknowledgement. Then the Ruby Sanctum stopped answering. The guards on the portal were dead, the mystic stones were shattered, and the red flight could not work out who had managed it — the black dragonflight's numbers in Northrend were nowhere near enough for an attack of that kind. What the attackers had come for was the red flight's eggs. Behind them was Halion, a twilight dragon, with General Zarithrian, Baltharus the Warborn and Saviana Ragefire between him and the door, and Sanctum Guardian Xerestrasza the only defender still standing. It did not end there. Once the Shattering had come and gone, the Twilight's Hammer arrived to corrupt what was kept in the chamber, and Korialstrasz destroyed himself and every sanctum at once to stop them, leaving nothing behind but traces of the energy he used. The Ruby Sanctum was later rebuilt, and it is where the last red dragon eggs were kept.
assumes: It assumes you ran the Obsidian Sanctum. This is the retaliation for that raid, and the two chambers are doors off the same corridor under Wyrmrest Temple.
disputed: The wiki hedges the rebuilding openly: the last red dragon eggs were probably moved here before the Dragon Soul raid, since the flight was sterile afterwards — or the eggs were elsewhere all along and the sanctum was rebuilt around them once it was clear there would be no more. It does not decide.
How the black dragonflight breached the sanctum undetected is posed as a question rather than answered, on the same page that names Halion as the one who did it.

summary: An arena rather than a fortress. Tirion Fordring built the Crusaders' Coliseum on the Argent Tournament grounds in Icecrown to work out who was fit to go into Icecrown Citadel, and the trial is the audition.
history: By this point the war in Northrend had gone well enough that only the citadel was left, and both Garrosh Hellscream and Varian Wrynn wanted to storm it. Tirion Fordring told them to wait. The Ebon Blade's death knights and the Argent Crusade had both spent weeks watching the Scourge from footholds near the citadel and, despite having every reason to distrust each other, reached the same conclusion: a mass assault was exactly what the Lich King was inviting, because everyone who died in it would stand up again on his side. What might work was a small strike force. To find one, Tirion held a tournament, and both factions trusted him to run it — he had held Light's Hope Chapel, and the Horde had not forgotten what he once gave up for an orc. The trial itself sends beasts of Northrend across the floor, then the eredar Lord Jaraxxus, then champions of the opposing faction fought as a team, then the Twin Val'kyr, and then the floor gives way and the raid is dropped on Anub'arak. Tirion got his champions, and the Ashen Verdict formed around them.
assumes: The raid never says why the Argent Crusade is holding a tournament in the middle of Scourge country. It is a selection process, and the reasoning behind it — that a frontal assault on Icecrown Citadel would hand the Lich King an army — is delivered somewhere else entirely.
disputed: The wiki's own infobox lists the raid's status as unavailable and on the public test realm, which is stale data rather than a description of anything.

Whether Anub'arak breaking through the coliseum floor is Scourge sabotage of the tournament or simply where the building happens to sit is never stated. The wiki records only that the raid is dropped in on him.
The heroic version is treated as a differently named raid, Trial of the Grand Crusader, rather than a difficulty of this one.

summary: The largest titan-forged complex on Azeroth, preserved in the snows of the Storm Peaks. Everyone who found it assumed a city, or a vault of relics. It is a prison, and what it was built to hold is the Old God Yogg-Saron.
history: Ulduar has never held Yogg-Saron completely. Its blood runs through the whole continent, crystallising as saronite, and its whispers travel with it — which is how the keeper Loken was turned. Odyn had already taken one wing away long before: he had Helya tear the Halls of Valor loose and set them in the sky for an army of his own. What mattered now was that Loken had relit the Forge of Wills and was producing iron dwarves and iron vrykul loyal to the thing below. Brann Bronzebeard came to Ulduar looking for dwarven history, barely got out, and told the Kirin Tor. Varian Wrynn and Garrosh Hellscream nearly killed each other in Dalaran arguing about what to do, so the expeditions went in separately and cooperated anyway. Yogg-Saron drove several of the attackers insane and turned them on their own side, and lost regardless. Then Loken's death tripped a titan failsafe, and Algalon the Observer arrived to authorise the scouring of Azeroth. He was not defeated so much as talked out of it: he had purged worlds before and had never considered that the life on them wanted to survive this badly.
assumes: You are expected to already know that the titans built Azeroth's keepers, and that Freya, Hodir, Thorim and Mimiron are on your side underneath what you are fighting. It also assumes you have run the Halls of Stone and the Halls of Lightning, which are other wings of the same building.
disputed: The wiki records that an unknown entity time-travelled to Ulduar to age the titan locks holding Yogg-Saron, releasing it forty millennia early, and that a bronze dragon arrived too late to prevent the change. Who did it is left blank.

Whether Yogg-Saron is contained or merely quiet is hedged after the fact: its corpse is still imprisoned and its influence seems contained, but its whispers are still reported around Northrend and in Ulduar's own halls.

summary: A titan vault under Wintergrasp Fortress, holding relics and four giants set to guard them. You can only get in while your faction holds Wintergrasp, which makes it the one raid in the game gated behind a battleground.
history: Wintergrasp is a plateau above the Dragonblight and the Borean Tundra that nobody had reason to visit for a very long time: titan fortifications, domed watchtowers, and wind going through them unheard. What changed that was elemental material in quantity and the strategic value of the fortifications themselves, and the plateau became a standing tug-of-war between the Horde and the Alliance. Under the keep is what the watchtowers were guarding. Its wardens were placed there to protect the relics inside and have been doing it without interruption ever since, and both factions breaking in on them has not improved anybody's temper. Archavon the Stone Watcher was found first; Emalon, Koralon and Toravon were each uncovered in turn as the war above ground on. Years later Wrathion came here hunting for a way to fight the Old Gods and found a great deal of material worth studying, guarded by giants who were still furious about the previous visitors.
assumes: Entry is a prize. You cannot get in unless your side won the last battle for Wintergrasp, and ten minutes before the next one starts every watcher not already in combat turns back to stone until it is over.
